Paul Graham is the co-founder of Y Combinator and one of the great philosophers of the computer science world. For 25 years he has been publishing thoughtful essays on his blog — though infrequently: in 2025, for instance, he published just four pieces. In March 2026 a new one appeared: «The Brand Age». I&rsquo;d like to discuss it.
Why does this matter to me? Among the writers I follow, Paul Graham comes first. I&rsquo;ve referenced his essays several times before — in my roundup of resources …
items.summary: Reflections on Paul Graham's essay "The Brand Age": why technological advantage is finite, and when betting on brand becomes a matter of survival.
items.title: The Brand Age, Paul Graham

The goal of strategy is to move from &laquo;we build whatever anyone asks for&raquo; to a considered position aimed at creating a better future for both users and the business.
As much as we&rsquo;d like one to exist, there is no universal product strategy template — no template at all, really. The format depends on the company&rsquo;s maturity, the team&rsquo;s experience, organizational structure, business model, business strategy, and a huge number of other factors.
That&rsquo;s precisely why …
items.summary: There's no universal product strategy template. On what strategy can look like in practice and why it's a living system, not a document.
items.title: Product Strategy ≠ Template

I came across an interesting approach to goal-setting — NCT (Narratives, Commitments, Tasks) by Ravi Mehta [1]. What makes it compelling is that it positions itself as an alternative to OKR and could be genuinely useful for many product teams. Before diving into NCT, let&rsquo;s take a quick look at the history of goal-setting frameworks.
In 1954, Peter Drucker introduced the concept of MBO (Management by Objectives) in his book The Practice of Management [2]. The core idea: set goals at the …

As someone who came up through the technical side, I long believed that &laquo;marketing&raquo; was limited to finding promotion channels, communicating product value to users, and selling goods — physical or digital, it didn&rsquo;t matter. But that understanding of marketing …

Loyalty Customer Loyalty is devotion to a brand or product. It means that when faced with comparable alternatives, a user will choose our product. This choice is often emotional — a user who loves a product will recommend it to friends and family.
The standard metric for measuring customer loyalty is the NPS (Net Promoter Score), whose growth positively correlates with sales growth and market share gains. This relationship, combined with how easy the metric is to measure, is exactly what made it …
items.summary: Why loyalty and satisfaction are different concepts, and how to measure them correctly using NPS and CSI.
items.title: Loyalty ≠ Satisfaction

Leadership is the skill of positively influencing people in a way that enables a group to achieve ambitious goals through the contribution of each individual …

Zettelkasten is an increasingly popular method of organizing notes and ideas, developed by the extraordinarily productive German sociologist Niklas Luhmann, who over his lifetime managed to write more than 70 major academic books and 500 scholarly articles, and received prestigious doctoral honors and prizes for his contributions to sociology.

A retrospective is a group reflection exercise — a tool for continuous improvement and cultural change within a team.
Most of us hear about &laquo;retros&raquo; in the context of end-of-sprint ceremonies in iterative development. However, the vast majority of teams don&rsquo;t follow Scrum or any iterative approach to building software products. That&rsquo;s no reason to abandon self-reflection or group reflection when you hit key project milestones.
Below is a detailed 8-step plan with timings …

items.title: How to Run a Retrospective for a Large Team
